portability: 1 · Tools
Ship one MCP server
MCP is the only substrate every host speaks. Claude Code can even serve its own tools (`claude mcp serve`); Codex cannot — so an MCP server is the only way to give Codex a tool set you control.
enact-agent has no server mode today. This is the single highest-leverage change for the 'one system' goal.
2 · Tools, take two
Or offer a tool-injection API

jcode's Harness API exposes `ConfigureTools { enabled, disabled, custom }`: an external client registers its own tool implementations, the model calls them, and the runtime routes the call back down that client's connection. The custom tool is an execution adapter only — it never enters the shared registry, so hooks, telemetry, output limits and permission gates behave exactly as for built-ins.
This is the richer alternative to MCP when you own the host: the tool implementations stay in your process, and the runtime keeps its safety model intact.
3 · Schema budget
Expose search + call, not N schemas

jcode collapses MCP servers into a fixed `mcp` / `mcp_search` / `mcp_call` surface with a 32-reference cap and a 6 000-token result budget; providers with native deferred loading get `defer_loading` instead. Claude Code has MCP Tool Search; oh-my-pi uses xd:// devices + BM25.
enact-agent already has `tool_search` and `mcp_deferred` — extend the same idea to MCP servers.
4 · Behaviour
Per-host hook dialects

lean-ctx is the reference: 17 hook actions rendered into 11 host dialects, each installer writing that host's own config file. jcode keeps it simpler — eight external-program hooks, one command per event.
Ship Claude Code `settings.json` and Codex `.codex/hooks.json` installers. Do not invent a new hook format.
5 · Instructions
AGENTS.md + SKILL.md

Codex reads AGENTS.md natively. Claude Code reads AGENTS.md only when no CLAUDE.md exists (v2.1.277+), or you put an `@path` import on line 1 of CLAUDE.md, or set project instructions to claude-md-and-agents-md.
One AGENTS.md, one SKILL.md, imported by both. AGENTS.md is capped at 32 KiB by default. jcode, goose and oh-my-pi all already read these paths.
6 · Policy
Degrade to each host's own rules
Codex uses `.rules` files (allow / prompt / forbidden). Claude Code uses permissions in settings.json. They are not the same model and should not be unified.
A shared tool must respect the host's policy rather than assume it. enact-agent's availability-vs-authorization split maps cleanly onto this.

jcode_facts: Language / licence
Rust (91.6% of the repo) · MIT · ~21k stars · single native binary, no Node or Python runtime
Registered tools
34 built-ins (27 base + 4 per-session + the `mcp` family + 2 desktop-only), plus dynamically registered `mcp__<server>__<tool>` proxies
Not registered

`ls`, `glob`, `grep`, `subagent`, `goal`, `plan`, `rewind`, `checkpoint` are NOT model-callable tools. `ls` and `grep` survive only as alias names; the `acp` and `minimal` tool profiles still list `ls`, which is a dangling reference. Rewind is a Harness API request, not a tool.
Harness API

Stable, versioned client API over a Unix socket, spoken as NDJSON. `API_VERSION_MAJOR` 1 / `API_VERSION_MINOR` 11. Every frame carries `v`; clients must ignore unknown fields and skip unknown event kinds. Explicitly the public boundary between the harness and any UI (TUI, desktop, web, scripts), and deliberately smaller than the internal `jcode-protocol`.
★ External tool injection

`ApiRequest::ConfigureTools { session_id, tools: ToolConfiguration }` carries `enabled`, `disabled` and `custom: Vec<SessionToolDefinition>`. A custom tool may override a built-in of the same name. The model calls it, the server emits a `ToolCall` event down the client's own connection, the client replies with `ToolResult` (120 s deadline). This is a complete, versioned contract for handing a tool set to a runtime from outside it.
★ Injected tools keep builtin semantics
A custom tool is an "execution adapter only, never installed in the shared registry" — so hooks, telemetry, output limits and permission gates behave exactly as they do for built-ins.
External-program hooks

Eight hook keys in `docs/HOOKS.md` — `pre_tool`, `pre_tool_transform`, `post_tool`, `post_tool_feedback`, `turn_start`, `turn_end`, `session_start`, `session_end`. Each is a command string or array; observers run in order, gates run sequentially and the first block wins. `post_tool_feedback` appends its stdout to the tool result, which is how linters and checkers feed findings back to the model.
MCP config interop

Project precedence: `.jcode/mcp.json` → `.mcp.json` (Claude Code) → `.claude/mcp.json`. Claude Code is a LIVE source (`~/.claude.json` and `~/.claude/mcp.json`) and is never copied. Codex is a one-time import from `~/.codex/config.toml` `[mcp_servers.*]`, and only while `~/.jcode/mcp.json` does not exist — the stated reason is that persisting a live source would resurrect deleted servers and duplicate inline secrets.
Server preference

Runnable wins. A remote twin of a working local stdio server does not overwrite it, because a remote twin usually needs a separate login. A broken higher-precedence entry does not shadow a working one.
Schema bloat control

Three layers: provider-native deferred loading (`defer_loading` + `cache_control`) where supported; a fixed `mcp` / `mcp_search` / `mcp_call` surface elsewhere; and transcript announcement for tools that arrive late. `mcp_search` caps at 32 tool references under a 6 000-token budget, drops description-only matches once a name matches, and trims descriptions before dropping schemas.
Prompt-cache safety

The tool list is locked after the first request. Exactly ONE deliberate rebuild is permitted, latched by a one-shot guard that is deliberately NOT re-armed. Definitions are sorted by name because ordering is a cache requirement. An AGENTS.md snapshot keeps the cacheable prefix stable when a tool edits it mid-session.
Advertise-early
Proxy tools are registered from the on-disk schema cache before connections settle, so the first locked snapshot already contains MCP tools and the intentional cache miss can be avoided entirely.
Tool profiles

`full` (default) | `acp` | `minimal` | `none`, plus explicit allow/deny lists, `disable_base_tools` and `mcp_tools = auto|eager|deferred`. Deny beats allow; `disabled: ["mcp"]` disables every MCP tool at once.
Canonical alias table

`resolve_tool_name()` maps every host's vocabulary onto one internal name — `Bash`, `file_grep`, `shell_exec`, `functions.bash`, `todoread`, `multiedit`, `patch`, `communicate` — with a matching provider-side reverse map.
Swarm

One tool (`communicate`, exposed as `swarm`). The server coordinates agents in the same repo: a `FileTouch` bus event detects contention and emits a `FileConflict` notification plus a soft interrupt to BOTH parties. Detection and notification only — no automatic merge; cross-agent write serialization is a process-local mutex.
Memory graph

A typed graph, not a key-value store: weighted edges, tag and cluster nodes, and `supersede` edges. Recall is link-traversal-capable (`related`, `link`, `tag`), so a memory can be found through its relationships and not only by similarity.
Providers

Anthropic (OAuth), OpenAI / Codex OAuth, Gemini, Copilot, OpenRouter, Antigravity, Bedrock, Cursor, Grok Build, plus a large OpenAI-compatible catalog. Anthropic OAuth beta headers deliberately do NOT claim `claude-code`.
Skills & extensions

Skills are Markdown + YAML frontmatter with `allowed-tools`, discovered from `.jcode/skills`, `.claude/skills` and `.agents/skills`, invoked as `/name`, overlaid per session at read time. Applets mount declarative native UI. Codemode is a QuickJS sandbox that can call any session tool.
